items.prompt: What is a 'race condition'?
choices: A bug where the correctness of a result depends on the relative timing of two or more operations on shared state
Any bug that only reproduces under heavy server load, regardless of how the operations are timed relative to each other
A deadlock where two threads are each permanently waiting on a resource the other one is holding
A memory leak caused by a program failing to release resources it had previously allocated
items.explanation: A race condition is specifically about timing-dependent correctness — the same code can produce a right or wrong result depending on how two operations happen to interleave.
items.reference:
Race condition
⏱️ Correctness depends on timing
🔀 Result varies with interleaving
Why: the operations are each correct alone — the bug lives in the ordering.
items.learnMore:
Timing is the bug, not the logic

A race condition is unusual among bugs: every line of code involved can be individually correct, and the program can still produce a wrong result, purely because of how two operations happened to interleave in time.

Common mistake

Looking for a race condition's cause inside one request's logic, instead of in how two requests' operations interleaved.
items.reflection: A race condition is really a special case of a more general trap: a result that depends on timing rather than logic feels deterministic until it isn't. Where else have you seen 'it worked every time I tried it' turn out to mean 'I never happened to try it at the unlucky moment'?

items.prompt: What is a 'critical section'?
choices: The span of code, from reading a shared value to finishing the update based on it, that must not be interrupted
Any function in the codebase that happens to take longer than 100 milliseconds to fully execute
The specific part of a program that is responsible for handling error logging and reporting
A section of code that is only ever executed once, during the server's own startup sequence
items.explanation: The critical section is the read-to-write span where an interruption from another operation touching the same shared value would corrupt the result.
items.reference:
Critical section
📖 Read shared value
✍️ ... act on it ...
🚫 Must not be interrupted in between
Why: this span is exactly where a race condition can slip in.
items.learnMore:
The span, not a single line

A critical section isn't one line of code — it's the whole stretch from the first read of a shared value to the last write based on that read. Any point inside that stretch is a place another operation's read can land and corrupt the result.

Common mistake

Thinking of the critical section as just the write statement, rather than the entire read-to-write span.
items.reflection: Naming the exact span that must not be interrupted is a recurring move in concurrent systems — transactions, locks, and atomic instructions all exist to protect some specific span, never the whole program. Where have you seen a system draw a deliberately narrow boundary around 'this part must not be interrupted' rather than protecting everything?

items.prompt: What does 'atomicity' guarantee about an operation?
choices: It happens as a single, indivisible step — nothing else can observe it half-done
It guarantees the operation will always finish executing in under one full millisecond of wall-clock time

items.explanation: Atomicity is about indivisibility from other operations' point of view, not about speed or reliability — an atomic operation can still fail, it just can't be observed partially done.
items.reference:
Atomicity
🧱 Indivisible from outside
🚫 No 'half-done' observable state
Why: atomicity closes the gap a race condition exploits, by removing the gap entirely.
items.learnMore:
Indivisible, not fast or infallible

Atomicity is purely about what other operations can observe — nothing else can see the operation half-done. An atomic operation can still fail outright; it just can't fail or succeed partway, where someone else's read could catch it mid-change.

Common mistake

Confusing atomicity with speed, reliability, or 'can't fail' — atomicity only promises indivisibility, nothing about outcome.
items.reflection: Atomicity's promise — complete it all, or let nobody see the middle — shows up anywhere a partial, visible intermediate state would mislead an observer: a bank transfer debiting one account before crediting another, a file save that could leave a half-written file on a crash. Where else does 'no visible middle state' matter more than speed?

items.prompt: What does a lock (mutex) do?
choices: Lets only one operation enter a critical section at a time, forcing others to wait their turn
Prevents a program from crashing outright whenever it's given some form of invalid input data
Encrypts a piece of shared data so that no other process on the machine is able to read it

items.explanation: A lock's job is serialization: it makes concurrent callers wait outside the critical section instead of interleaving into it.
items.reference:
Lock (mutex)
🔒 One caller in the critical section
⏳ Others wait their turn
Why: a lock fixes races by serializing access, not by removing the gap.
items.learnMore:
Serialize, don't remove

A lock doesn't make the critical section disappear or collapse into one step the way atomicity does — it keeps the gap exactly as it was, and instead forces every other caller to wait outside it until the current holder finishes.

Common mistake

Assuming a lock closes the TOCTOU gap the same way atomicity does — a lock serializes access to the gap, it doesn't remove the gap.
items.reflection: A lock trades throughput for generality: it works for any critical section, no matter how complex, at the cost of making other callers wait. Where else in systems (or outside them) have you seen the same trade — a more general solution that costs something a narrower, specialized one wouldn't?

items.prompt: Implement `Mutex.acquire()`, matching L3: it returns a `Promise`. If the mutex isn't locked, lock it (`this.locked = true`) and resolve immediately. If it's already locked, push the resolver onto `this.queue` instead of resolving yet, so the caller waits until `release()` hands it the lock.

items.reference:
Mutex mechanics
🔓 Unlocked → resolve immediately
🔒 Locked → queue the resolver
Why: the queue is what makes waiters resolve in order, one at a time.

Mutex mechanics

Hand-off, not just unlock

If release() only set `locked = false`, a brand-new acquire() call could win the lock before an already-queued waiter gets a turn. Calling the queued resolver directly skips that race entirely by never actually unlocking in between.
